summary.text: For \(n=9\), the product of the first nine primes is \(223092870\), and \(223092870^2+1=49770428644836901=29^2\cdot 59180057841661\). Thus this term is not squarefree, so the conjunction fails regardless of the claim about infinitely many prime terms.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,\ldots\) be the primes in increasing order, and put
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\qquad
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
We disprove the assertion that every \(a(n)\) is squarefree by exhibiting a single term divisible by the square of a prime.

Take \(n=9\). The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Their successive products are
\[
2,\ 6,\ 30,\ 210,\ 2310,\ 30030,\ 510510,\ 9699690,\ 223092870,
\]
so
\[
P_9=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23
   =223092870.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
  &=223092870^2+1\\
  &=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now \(29\) is prime: since \(\sqrt{29}<6\), a nontrivial factorization of \(29\) would have a prime factor among \(2,3,5\), but \(29\) is divisible by none of these. We show that \(29^2\) divides \(a(9)\). Since \(29^2=841\), direct division of the primorial gives
\[
223092870=841\cdot265270+800.
\]
Thus
\[
P_9\equiv800\equiv-41\pmod{841}.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(9)=P_9^2+1\equiv(-41)^2+1=1682=2\cdot841\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
Hence \(29^2\mid a(9)\). Equivalently, the exact divisibility can be seen from
\[
49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901
 =841\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661
 =29^2\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661.
\]

An integer is squarefree precisely when it is not divisible by the square of any prime. Since the prime square \(29^2\) divides \(a(9)\), the term \(a(9)\) is not squarefree. Therefore the universal claim
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\quad a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
is false.

The conjecture in question is the conjunction of this universal squarefreeness claim and the claim that \(a(n)\) is prime for infinitely many \(n\). A conjunction is false whenever either of its components is false. The counterexample \(n=9\) already falsifies its first component, independently of whether infinitely many terms are prime. Thus the stated combined conjecture is false.
